segments.say: At midnight on January 1st, 2027, every product in California with Red No. 3 becomes illegal to sell. No grace period.
The dye hides under many names. Stores get one night.

Reading a label decides what's pulled. What's pulled decides which shelves, which people, which shifts, which substitutes, which trucks. Change one rule and it ripples through all of them. A system like this has to agree with itself, everywhere at once.
segments.beat: Every part depends on every other

segments.say: So we asked Gemini 4 Argon to write the whole system in one continued generation: one author, holding every part in mind at once.
646,825 tokens. 911 files. Ten hops, nine hand-offs, every one clean.
After a one-line fix, all 6,581 cross-file links line up. One mis-indented line near token 132,000 stopped the label package loading; the managed agent fixed it in 21 seconds.
A test written at token 641,687 calls a function Argon wrote 552,000 tokens earlier.
That's what a million-token model is for: the whole system in one head.

But consistent code isn't correct code. Our verifier found 21,459 plan mistakes: people double-booked, tasks outside the shift. Each row here is one simulated associate: 7,161 double-bookings, and 14,117 tasks outside the 10 PM to 6 AM shift.

A managed agent traced it to one root cause, one shared time cursor for all associates, and fixed it. Scheduling mistakes went from 21,284 to zero, even in 10 stores it never saw. Plan mistakes went from 21,459 to 175: 12 missed products and 3 look-alikes, still open.
And the working core Argon wrote this morning, on 20 stores, overnight: tags flash, associates walk to each shelf, and every store goes green.

With three small logged fixes to its first draft, it found all 467 products with Red No. 3, pulled none of the 483 look-alikes, covered every one of 6,718 shelf spots, and finished every task before midnight.
When a law changes overnight, you don't have months. Argon writes the whole system at once, the verifier proves it, the agent repairs it.
